items.why: Clearly distinguishes the five men taking the objects from the priest and armed men stationed outside.
“What happens first?” invites “they are taken,” which does not distinguish the five men from the priest.
Tests who “our” refers to, but “Whose ruler” makes that distinction unnecessarily awkward.
Separates the land’s abundance as the cause of prosperity from the comparison with Sidonian security.
Tests the explicit reason for seeking territory rather than confusing it with Israel’s lack of a king.
Clearly identifies fear of Abimelek as Jotham’s reason for living away, rather than later hostility involving Shechem.
Distinguishes the relatives asked to relay Abimelek’s message from the citizens meant to receive it.
Separates the Levite’s open-ended search for lodging from the house he encounters along the way.
Calls a conditional blessing a “request” and tests its position rather than the blessing-versus-curse distinction.
“Does something” removes the meaningful hiring event and leaves an opaque beneficiary-identification task.
“People coming out of the city” could broadly paraphrase the reported trip to the fields, weakening the answer contrast.
Distinguishes the mother’s stated plan for her son from the silversmith’s subsequent work.
Requires tracking who is run through and dies, rather than confusing the servant with his victim.
Directly tests the lethal fire rather than confusing the occupants’ refuge with the means of their deaths.
Separates the duration of the family’s priestly service from the differently bounded use of Micah’s idol.
Shouting is the immediate cue, but being overtaken also plausibly contributes to the Danites’ turn.
The fruit-versus-rule tradeoff is clear, but duplicates the olive-tree question’s refusal logic.
Burning is the specific doorway goal, but “attacking” remains a compatible broader answer.
“Take over” can naturally cover both the land and its inhabitants, blurring the proposed distinction.
Tests Micah’s stated religious confidence in having a Levite priest, not an incidental detail about the Levite’s origin.
The hill country contains Micah’s house; treating it as a separate preceding stop makes “just before” unstable.
Resolves the person owed fair treatment as Jerub-Baal, whose rescue supplies the reason for that obligation.
Clearly distinguishes Zebul, the secret message’s sender, from Gaal, the opponent described in it.
Tests the important distinction between the priest asked to inquire and God as the source of guidance.
“After” falsely turns the curse’s fulfillment into a separate event following God’s punishment.
Distinguishes Zebul’s claim about shadows from Gaal’s report of approaching people.
Separates Jotham’s stated purpose for listening—God hearing the citizens—from the king-making story that follows.
Tests the valued contribution behind the olive tree’s rhetorical refusal, rather than treating the next invitation as its cause.
Requires identifying the mother’s earlier curse within Micah’s speech, despite her present words being a blessing.
Clearly locates the denunciation during festival eating and drinking, not the preceding grape harvest.
Tests isolation as the reason rescue is unavailable, rather than confusing the attack itself with that explanation.
